DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 09/28/2023 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.           Regarding Claims 1, Applicant argues that in the Examiner Interview it was agreed between the Applicant and Examiner that Huber fails to disclose or contemplate a topskin coupled to the first top mating surface and the second top mating surface of the first tray and the topskin further coupled to the first top mating surface and the second top mating surface of the second tray. In response, Examiner would like to note that the Examiner Interview consisted of discussing possible amendments and clarifications to the claims in regards to the connections between the topskin and mating surfaces but it was not agreed that these amendments would traverse the rejection. Regarding the amendments of Claim 1, Examiner would like to make reference to Marked up Figure 2 of Huber (US 7,556,462) shown below. Pointed out by arrows, each tray (10) contains a First and Second top mating surface on the flanges, a similar structure to Applicants Flanges and Mating surfaces as shown in Figure 3B of the claimed invention. Figure 3 of Huber shows how these flanges are used as the connection surfaces between the tray (10) and the topskin (53), and is further disclosed in the specification that the ball elements (53) are attached to mounting rails within the mounting profiles (10) (Column 3, lines 25-26). Further, Figure 1 of Huber shows how the topskin elements (ball elements 53 and ball mats 21) are coupled to the first and second top mating surfaces of each tray (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) to create a contiguous sheet of topskin, and that the trays are disposed underneath the topskin in order to allow for the conveying of articles across the rollers.
Regarding Claim 8, Applicant argues that in the Examiner Interview it was agreed between the Applicant and Examiner that Huber fails to disclose or contemplate a topskin coupled to the first and second top mating surfaces of each tray in the plurality of trays. In response, Examiner would like to note that the Examiner Interview consisted of discussing possible amendments and clarifications to the claims in regards to the connections between the topskin and mating surfaces but it was not agreed that these amendments would traverse the rejection. Regarding the amendments of Claim 8, Examiner would like to make reference to Figure 3 and Marked up Figure 2 of Huber. Marked up Figure 2 shows how the Flanges comprise a top mating surface, and Figure 3 shows how each portion of the topskin (Ball elements 53 and Ball mats 21) are connected by these surfaces. Figure 1 further shows how the topskin (Ball elements 53 and Ball mats 21) utilizes the mounting surfaces of each tray along a plurality of trays in order to create a contiguous surface for workpieces to be conveyed over.
Regarding Claim 15, Applicant argues that in the Examiner Interview it was agreed between the Applicant and Examiner that Huber fails to disclose or contemplate wherein the plurality of trays are contiguously covered over an entirety of the plurality of tray. In response, Examiner would like to note that the Examiner Interview consisted of discussing possible amendments and clarifications to the claims in regards to the connections between the topskin and mating surfaces but it was not agreed that these amendments would traverse the rejection. Regarding the amendments of Claim 15, Examiner would like to make reference to Figure 1 of Huber. The ball elements (53) and the ball mats (21) contiguously create a covering or topskin over the trays (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) by being interconnected throughout the trays in order to allow for workpieces to move over the top (Column 3, lines 19-26). Figure 1 shows how the topskin can be composed over a plurality of trays to create the conveying area of the workpieces, and is covered over the entirety of the trays in the conveying section, wherein Huber shows an additional benefit with trays also being able to hold floor plates (20).
Regarding Claims 1-16 and 18-21, Applicant does not provide any arguments based upon the claim’s respective rejections other than to state these claim rejections should be traversed under the Amended Claims 1, 8 and 15.
For the foregoing reasons, the claims stand rejected.

Drawings
The drawings were received on 09/28/2023.  These drawings are acceptable to cover the objection regarding reference characters 516 and 616.
The drawings are objected to as failing to comply with 37 CFR 1.84(p)(5) because they do not include the following reference sign(s) mentioned in the description: Mating Surfaces 342 and 352.  Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
(a)(2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), in which the patent or application, as the case may be, names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claims 1-10, 13, 15-16 and 21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Huber (United States Patent US 7,556,462 B2).

Regarding Claim 1, Huber discloses a cargo handling system (Column 1, lines 17-18: “cargo deck for a cargo hold”), comprising: a first tray (Figure 1: Profile 10-1) extending longitudinally from a first longitudinal end to a second longitudinal end (Figure 1: Left end to right end of Profile 10-1); a second tray disposed laterally adjacent to the first tray (Figure 1: Profile 10-2), the first tray and the second tray (Figure 1: Profiles 10-1, 10-2) each including a first flange defining a first top mating surface and a second flange defining a second top mating surface (Column 3, lines 25-26: “ball elements 53 are attached to mounting rails within the mounting profiles 10”, wherein Figure 3 shows the connection of the ball element 53, further showing the left side rail of profile 10 as the first flange/mating surface, and the right side rail as the second flange/mating surface and Marked up Figure 2 shows the first and second top mating surfaces); and a topskin coupled to (Figure 1: Ball Elements 53) the first top mating surface and the second top mating surface of the first tray, the topskin further coupled to the first top mating surface and the second top mating surface tray (Figure 3: Shows how Ball Elements 53 are comprised within the first and second mating surfaces of each tray, and further Figure 1 shows ball mats 21 disposed in-between trays to inter-connect) wherein the first tray and the second tray are disposed below the topskin (Figure 1: Shows ball elements 53 and ball mats 21 coupled to the first and second top mating surfaces of each tray (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) to create a contiguous sheet of topskin, and that the trays are disposed underneath the topskin in order to allow for the conveying of articles across the roller).
Regarding Claim 2, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 1, as seen above. Huber further discloses further comprising a roller assembly (Figure 3: Rollers 31-34, and Ball rollers in Ball Elements 53) coupled to the topskin (Figure 3: Ball Elements 53) and disposed within the first tray (Figure 1: Profile 10-1).
Regarding Claim 3, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 1, as seen above. Huber further discloses wherein the topskin extends laterally contiguously from the first top mating surface of the first tray, to the second top mating surface of the first tray, to the first top mating surface of the  second tray, to the second top mating surface of the second tray (Figure 3: Shows how Ball Elements 53 are comprised within the first and second mating surfaces of each tray, and further Figure 1 shows ball elements 53 and ball mats 21 coupled to the first and second top mating surfaces of each tray (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) to create a contiguous sheet of topskin).
Regarding Claim 4, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 1, as seen above. Huber further discloses further comprising a ball transfer unit (BTU) (Figure 3: Ball transfers composed within Ball Elements 53) coupled to the topskin (Figure 3: Ball Elements 53) and disposed within the first tray (Figure 1: Profile 10-1).
Regarding Claim 5, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 1, as seen above. Huber further discloses further comprising a power drive unit (PDU) (Figure 1: Power Drive Units (PDU) 51) disposed between the first tray and the second tray (Figure 1: Shows PDUs 51 disposed between each tray).
Regarding Claim 6, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 1, as seen above. Huber further discloses wherein the first tray and the second tray are contiguously covered (Figure 1: Trays are covered by Ball Mats 21 and Ball elements 53) over an entirety of the first tray and the second tray (Figure 1: Shows the topskin composed over a plurality of trays (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) to create the conveying area of the workpieces (area by door region 55), and is covered over the entirety of the trays in the conveying section).
Regarding Claim 7, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 1, as seen above. Huber further discloses wherein: the first tray and the second tray each comprise a base (Marked up Figure 2: Base), a first sidewall extending from the base to the first flange (Marked up Figure 2: First wall), a second sidewall extending from the base to the second flange (Marked up Figure 2: Second wall), and the first sidewall, the second sidewall, and the base (Marked up Figure 2: Base, First and Second Wall) defining a groove configured to receive at least one of a ball transfer unit (BTU) and a roller assembly (Figures 2 and 3: Shows how the groove created by the First Wall, Second Wall and Base contain the Rollers 31-34, and Ball rollers in Ball Elements 53).
Regarding Claim 8, Huber discloses a cargo handling system (Column 1, lines 17-18: “cargo deck for a cargo hold”), comprising, a plurality of trays (Figure 1: Profiles 10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3); each of the plurality of trays comprising a base (Marked up Figure 2: Base), a first sidewall extending from the base to a first flange (Marked up Figure 2: First wall), a second sidewall extending from the base to a second flange (Marked up Figure 2: Second wall), the first flange extending outward in a first direction from the first sidewall (Marked up Figure 2: Shows first flange extending to the left from the first wall), the second flange extending outward in a second direction from the second sidewall the second direction opposite the first direction (Marked up Figure 2: Shows second flange extending to the right from the second wall), the first flange defining a first top mating surface, the second flange defining a second top mating surface (Marked up Figure 2: Shows the first and second top mating surface); a topskin (Figure 1: Ball Mats 21 and Ball elements 53) coupled to the first top mating surface and the second top mating surface of each of the plurality of trays (Figure 3 and Marked up Figure 2: Shows trays and first and second top mating surfaces covered by Ball Mats 21 and Ball elements 53), wherein the first sidewall, the second sidewall, the base and the topskin at least partially define a hollow chamber (Marked up Figure 2: Shows a hollowed surface in-between walls of the trays), and wherein each of the plurality of trays is disposed below the topskin (Figure 1: Shows ball elements 53 and ball mats 21 coupled to the first and second top mating surfaces of each tray (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) to create a contiguous sheet of topskin, and that the trays are disposed underneath the topskin in order to allow for the conveying of articles across the roller); a roller assembly (Figure 3: Rollers 31-34, and Ball rollers in Ball Elements 53) coupled, and disposed partially within, the hollow chamber (Figure 1: Shows Rollers 31-34, and Ball rollers in Ball Elements 53 disposed within Ball Elements 53 and Ball Mats 21), the roller assembly comprising: a fitting including a flange and a roller housing (Figure 3: Flange (Shown by circle surrounding ball rollers) and housing of Ball rollers composed within Ball Elements 53 and Ball Mats 21), the flange including a bottom surface mated to a top surface of the topskin (Figure 3: Flange (Circle surrounding Ball rollers on Ball elements 53) has its bottom surface mated to the top surface of Ball elements 53); and a roller rotatably coupled to the roller housing (Figure 3: Ball rollers of Ball elements 53 coupled to housing within).
Regarding Claim 9, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 8, as seen above. Huber further discloses wherein the roller assembly is disposed in a groove defined by a first tray in the plurality of trays (Figures 2 and 3 and Marked up Figure 2: Shows how the groove created by the First Wall, Second Wall and Base contain the Rollers 31-34, and Ball rollers in Ball Elements 53).
Regarding Claim 10, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 8, as seen above. Huber further discloses further comprising a plurality of the roller assembly (Figure 1: Shows a plurality of the roller assemblies in the Cargo deck 50).
Regarding Claim 13, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 8, as seen above. Huber further discloses wherein the plurality of trays are contiguously covered (Figure 1: Trays are covered by Ball Mats 21 and Ball elements 53).
Regarding Claim 15, Huber discloses a cargo handling system (Column 1, lines 17-18: “cargo deck for a cargo hold”), comprising: a plurality of trays (Figure 1: Profiles 10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3); a topskin (Figure 1: Ball Mats 21 and Ball elements 53) coupled to a top portion of each of the plurality of trays (Figure 1: Trays are covered by Ball Mats 21 and Ball elements 53); a ball transfer unit (BTU) coupled, and disposed partially within, the topskin (Figure 3: Ball transfers composed within Ball Elements 53), the BTU comprising: a retaining fixture including a flange and a housing (Figure 3: Flange (Shown by circle surrounding ball rollers) and housing of Ball rollers composed within Ball Elements 53 and Ball Mats 21), the flange mated to the topskin (Figure 3: Flange (Circle surrounding Ball rollers on Ball elements 53) has its bottom surface mated to the top surface of Ball elements 53); and a spherical ball disposed partially within the housing (Figure 3: Ball rollers of Ball elements 53 disposed partially within housing), wherein: the plurality of trays are contiguously covered over an entirety of the plurality of trays, and each of the plurality of trays is disposed below the topskin (Figure 1: Shows the topskin composed over a plurality of trays (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) to create the conveying area of the workpieces (area by door region 55), and is covered over the entirety of the trays in the conveying section).
Regarding Claim 16, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 15, as seen above. Huber further discloses wherein the housing of the retaining fixture is disposed at least partially within a first tray in the plurality of trays (Figure 3: Shows housing of Ball rollers of Ball Elements 53 partially disposed in profile 10).
Regarding Claim 21, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 15, as seen above. Huber further discloses wherein the topskin is configured to form a contiguous flat floor (Figure 1: Shows ball elements 53 and ball mats 21 coupled to the first and second top mating surfaces of each tray (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) to create a contiguous sheet of topskin) through a cargo compartment (Figure 1: Cargo deck 50).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 11, 12 and 18 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Huber (United States Patent US 7,556,462 B2) in view of Huber (United States Patent 6,125,984 A) .
Claims 14, 19 and 20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Huber (United States Patent US 7,556,462 B2) in view of Schoen (United States Patent Application US 2017/0313423 A1).
Regarding Claim 11, Huber (US 7,556,462 B2) discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 8, as seen above. Huber further discloses the fitting (Figure 3: Flange (Shown by circle surrounding ball rollers) and housing of Ball rollers composed within Ball Elements 53 and Ball Mats 21).
However, Huber does not disclose wherein the fitting further comprises a tab.
Huber (US 6,125,984 A) teaches a similar cargo handling system (Column 1, lines 4-6: “a ball mat for the loading deck of an aircraft, to support cargo and assist the movement thereof.”) wherein the fitting further comprises a tab (Figure 2: Annular Projection 29).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified Huber (US 7,556,462 B2) to incorporate the fitting tab as taught by Huber (US 6,125,984 A). The motivation for the modification would have been to make the ball mat more resistant, stiffer without adding weight, splash proof/ water-repellent and to overall allow loads on the mat to be more uniformly distributed (Column 1, lines 18-27 and lines 44-47).
Regarding Claim 12, Huber (US 7,556,462 B2)  in view of Huber (US 6,125,984 A) discloses the cargo handling system of claim 11, as seen above. Huber (US 6,125,984 A) further discloses wherein the fitting is configured to be press fit into the topskin (Figure 7: Shows the fitting configured to press fit into cover 11), the tab configured to couple the fitting to the topskin (Column 3, lines 43-47: “The holder 13 for the ball element 15, which is indicated only schematically in FIG. 2, stands on the floor plate 12 by way of devices including an annular projection 29 or a circumferential collar.”).
Regarding Claim 18, Huber (US 7,556,462 B2) discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 15, as seen above. Huber further discloses the retaining fixture (Figure 3: Shows housing of Ball rollers of Ball Elements 53 disposed in Profile 10).
However, Huber does not disclose wherein the retaining fixture is configured to be press fit into the topskin.
Huber (US 6,125,984 A) teaches a similar cargo handling system (Column 1, lines 4-6: “a ball mat for the loading deck of an aircraft, to support cargo and assist the movement thereof.”) wherein the retaining fixture is configured to be press fit into the topskin (Figure 7: Shows the fitting configured to press fit into cover 11, wherein Column 3, lines 43-47: “The holder 13 for the ball element 15, which is indicated only schematically in FIG. 2, stands on the floor plate 12 by way of devices including an annular projection 29 or a circumferential collar.”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified Huber (US 7,556,462 B2) to incorporate the press fit of the retaining fixture as taught by Huber (US 6,125,984 A). The motivation for the modification would have been to make the ball mat more resistant, stiffer without adding weight, splash proof/ water-repellent and to overall allow loads on the mat to be more uniformly distributed (Column 1, lines 18-27 and lines 44-47).
Regarding Claim 14, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 8, as seen above.
However, Huber does not disclose wherein the plurality of trays are made of a composite material.
Schoen teaches a similar cargo handling system (Figure 1: System 10) wherein the plurality of trays are made of a composite material (¶0008, lines 2-4: “This floor may comprise all suitable materials that withstand the gravitational forces of the loads, such as metal, plastic or composite materials”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified Huber to incorporate the composite material as taught by Schoen. The motivation for the modification would have been to allow the system to withstand the gravitational forces of the loads (¶0008, lines 2-4), which can allow for economical operation and as efficient loading and unloading of loads as possible (¶0006, lines 1-3).
Regarding Claim 19, Huber discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 15, as seen above.
However, Huber does not disclose wherein the plurality of trays are made of a composite material.
Schoen teaches a similar cargo handling system (Figure 1: System 10) wherein the plurality of trays are made of a composite material (¶0008, lines 2-4: “This floor may comprise all suitable materials that withstand the gravitational forces of the loads, such as metal, plastic or composite materials”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified Huber to incorporate the composite material as taught by Schoen. The motivation for the modification would have been to allow the system to withstand the gravitational forces of the loads (¶0008, lines 2-4), which can allow for economical operation and as efficient loading and unloading of loads as possible (¶0006, lines 1-3).
Regarding Claim 20, Huber in view of Schoen discloses the cargo handling system of Claim 19, as seen above. Schoen further discloses wherein the topskin comprises a metal top surface (¶0013, lines 1-5: “The guideway may, in general, comprise the same materials as the cargo compartment floor, and, in particular, materials that allow a, preferably, low-loss movement of the transport vehicle along the guideway, such as metal, plastic or composite materials.”) and a composite structure disposed below the metal top surface (¶0008, lines 2-4: “This floor may comprise all suitable materials that withstand the gravitational forces of the loads, such as metal, plastic or composite materials”, wherein the top and bottom structures can be comprised of any of these items).
Conclusion
THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL.  Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).
A shortened statutory period for reply to this final action is set to expire THREE MONTHS from the mailing date of this action.  In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action.  In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the mailing date of this final action.
